flagged.evidence: Claim 3 is false. On [0,1], let F(x)=x for x<=1/2 and F(x)=x+1 for x>1/2. This F is strictly increasing; the published definition says “increasing, or strictly increasing, when f(x)<f(y)” (def-monotone-function). Here beta_a=0 and F(t)-F(t^-)=0 for every t, so the displayed definition gives J_F=0 and C_F=F. But C_F has a right discontinuity at 1/2, contradicting “C_F is ... continuous on [a,b].”

Condition 2 requires the cheap subcover to be a subfamily of the given fine cover V. The step obtains disjoint J_n from V, but then says “Cover the null remainder ... by intervals (K_n)” and declares “(J_n) together with (K_n)” to be the required subcover. No assertion puts K_n in V, so this does not establish condition 2.

The step says an arbitrary monotone F may be assumed “increasing” and then invokes the jump-split theorem. But the published definition makes increasing strict, while monotone includes nondecreasing functions; F=0 is monotone and neither it nor -F is increasing. Moreover the cited split theorem's asserted continuous C_F is refuted by the strictly increasing right-jump example above. Thus the cited result does not license the asserted decomposition for the stated hypothesis.

The same inference is invalid here: the Statement permits every monotone F, but the proof replaces it by an “increasing” one and cites the split theorem. The disk definition says increasing means strictly increasing, so constant F is already outside that reduction; and the cited theorem's claim that C_F is continuous fails for a strictly increasing right-jump function.

The Statement requires A, J, and S all to be “increasing,” which the published definition identifies with strict increase. Take F(x)=x on [0,1], which is increasing and right-continuous. Its jump function is J_F=0, since beta_0=0 and every left-jump summand F(t)-F(t^-) is zero. Therefore no asserted triple can have J=J_F and have J increasing. Independently, the stated uniqueness omits the basepoint normalizations used in the proof, so constant transfers between A and S would also defeat uniqueness under a weak-increase reading.

The density theorem cited here begins “Let E subset of R^n be Lebesgue measurable.” This proof merely defines E_{r,R} through Dini derivatives and never proves it measurable. The published measure definition says “Lebesgue measure is the restriction lambda_n := lambda_n^* restriction L(R^n),” so lambda(E_{r,R} cap [u,v]) and the density-theorem invocation require that missing fact.

The cited Fubini theorem assumes “a sequence ... of increasing functions,” and the published definition makes increasing strict. But this step's c_n is explicitly “0 on [0,u_n]” and “1 on [v_n,1],” so c_n is not strictly increasing. Thus that theorem cannot be applied to conclude S'=0 almost everywhere.

The counterexample must satisfy the Statement's “increasing” hypothesis. The cited published Cantor corollary explicitly says: “The Cantor function is not strictly monotone ... it is nondecreasing but not increasing.” Thus c is outside the quantifier domain fixed by def-monotone-function, and does not refute the written statement.

It claims every summand x ↦ 1_{q_n<=x}2^{-n} is “increasing.” Under the published definition, increasing means strict; each such step function is constant on nonempty intervals and is only nondecreasing. The conclusion that J is strictly increasing is true because rationals are dense, but that needed argument is absent before Step 3.1 invokes a theorem whose hypothesis is increasing.

The recursive construction presumes an infinite sequence of remaining disjoint candidates. For E={0} and V={[−1/n,1/n]: n>=1}, V is fine but every two members intersect; after choosing I_1 no I_2 exists. The proof nevertheless asserts I_1,I_2,... and Step 2.1 uses their tails. A terminating selection case is not handled.
